Annie Pisuktie : la force d’une aînée: Annie Pisuktie: the strength of an elder
Nous avons rencontré l’aînée inuk Annie: We met Inuk elder Annie Pisuktie, who founded the Southern Quebec Inuit Association (SQIA) in 2017 with her daughter.
Annie Pisuktie prépare de la viande de p: Annie Pisuktie prepares seal meat for a meal. Photo credit: Maïssem Sahraoui
Je suis stagiaire à La Converse cet été,: I'm an intern at La Converse this summer, and this is my first published article! Along with my colleague Maïssem, I went to meet Annie Pisuktie, a truly endearing woman. Her daughter, Tina, suggested we profile her to highlight the role of older people in Indigenous communities, and also to showcase some of the interesting initiatives their members are leading. Annie's journey is indeed very inspiring.
Comme c’est mon premier long reportage,: Since this is my first long-form piece, I was very apprehensive while writing it. School and the field can sometimes be pretty different! I was used to writing shorter articles. As a result, finishing this one took me a little longer than planned. But we got there!
<strong>Annie Pisuktie est l’aînée de l’: Annie Pisuktie is the elder of the Southern Quebec Inuit Association (SQIA), which she founded in 2017 with her daughter Tina. It's a gathering place for Inuit in the city. From Iqaluit to Montréal, Annie has always cared deeply about the well-being of her people. We met this pillar of community work, along with several members of her association, so she could tell us her story.
Dans l’entrée du bâtiment situé à Pointe: In the entrance of the building in Pointe-Saint-Charles, a glass cabinet holds hats, jewellery and gloves, all made by Inuit artisans. To the right, a chart titled Inuktitut Syllabic shows the sounds and symbols used to write Inuktitut.
C’est ici que nous retrouvons Annie, ce: This is where we meet Annie on June 19. It's a prep day for a communal meal at the SQIA. Annie arrives a few minutes after noon. She starts the coffee machine and goes straight to join an employee who has already started cutting seal meat. She quickly pulls on blue gloves and her apron, which was surely white once. Every Thursday, any Inuk who wants to connect with members of the community can come to the association and enjoy a traditional meal. Seal, beluga, caribou… the fish and meat that get cooked are flown in directly from the North.
Derrière l’accueil, les usagers commence: Behind the reception desk, people start coming in. Some are in wheelchairs; others have intellectual disabilities. In the North, access to health care (in fact, to care of any kind) is limited. Many are therefore forced to move south, including to Quebec, at the risk of ending up isolated and far from their loved ones.
Dans la pièce principale, tout le monde: In the main room, everyone greets each other. Seated at a table, Annie picks up an uluk, a tool used to cut meat. There's a closeness between the visitors and the staff, who check in on the newcomers. Tina, Annie's daughter, jokes around with one of the regulars. An employee pats a regular on the shoulders.
L’odeur de la soupe aux légumes et au ph: The smell of the vegetable and seal soup Annie is heating drifts toward the noses of those chatting with their tablemates, coffee in hand, not to mention the aroma of the bread, the bannock, that Verna, an employee, is dropping into the oil.
Le bannock est un mélange de farine, de: Bannock is a mixture of flour, baking powder, salt and water. Photo credit: Maïssem Sahraoui
Malgré l’agitation du moment, et son emp: Despite the bustle of the moment, and what we can tell is a busy schedule, Annie sits down with us for an interview in an office. Seated next to her daughter Tina, she tells us her story, starting with her birth in Iqaluit, Nunavut. When she was three, she continues, her mother was often away from her to work at the hospital. The little girl was looked after by her great-aunts, her brother and other relatives. “The community took care of me,” she explains. “My mother passed away when I was very young, so I grew up with my stepfather, my half-sister and my brother.”
Elle se marie très jeune et a deux enfan: She married very young and had two children. Her marriage was an ordeal; Annie was a victim of domestic violence, she says, her throat tight and her eyes wet. “He was an alcoholic, six years older than me. My eldest was four and I told myself: ‘I don't want her to see me [with bruises].’”
Très jeune, elle rêve de la métropole. «: From a very young age, she dreamed of the big city. “I used to say: ‘I'm going to live in Montréal and I'm going to become a nurse.’” Later, when her second daughter needed medical care, she went to Montréal and realized she could stay in the city. “I can find myself a job!” She still seems amazed, 44 years later, when she talks about arriving in the city. “I was an interpreter for years at the Baffin Health Care Canada hospital, [...] for the courts, for youth protection, I was an interpreter everywhere.”
Parallèlement, Annie est aussi animatric: At the same time, Annie also hosted a show on CKUT radio for five years straight. Some people she knew hadn't heard from their families in a long time. “I wanted to make sure I went out into the community to record them, so their families could hear their voices.”
Si aujourd’hui l’AISQ existe, c’est grâc: If the SQIA exists today, it's thanks to Tina. Eight years ago, as she was graduating from university, her mother asked her to start an organization for Inuit in the city. “Everything is so far apart, we don't get the chance to connect like in the North, where communities are small,” she says. “Here, [...] events are rare. They make a big difference, Inuit can get together, have fun, play games, dance, the kids have a good time [...], it's a family. That's what's great about the SQIA.” The organization now has 11 employees, but people have been coming for so long that they pitch in too.
Annie et Tina Pisuktie. Crédit photo : M: Annie and Tina Pisuktie. Photo credit: Maïssem Sahraoui
Annie est la seule aînée au centre. Elle: Annie is the only elder at the centre. She explains that in Montréal, “older people are rare.” Not just any older person can be called an elder (or “aîné” in French), because that person has to “actively contribute to the community,” Tina clarifies. The role of an elder, we're told, is to teach culture, language and values to the youngest members of the community.
Tina interroge sa mère du regard, incert: Tina looks to her mother, unsure of the right pronunciation of what she's about to say in Inuktitut. “We have Inuit Qauijimajatuqangit, the values passed down by elders.” These teachings help people grow, to be good people who serve their community, she explains. “The teaching happens through stories that are passed down, that help people find their own path [...], that show that the road you choose isn't set in stone. It's gentle parenting.”
Travailler aux côtés de sa mère, coordon: Working alongside her mother, running an organization together, might seem complicated. “It's harder to take advice from your parents than from strangers, that's for sure!” says Tina, while Annie admits she's a strict mother. “I have a huge amount of respect for her,” Tina continues. Their motherly pride and closeness are obvious. Annie showers her daughter with compliments like “my beautiful young lady” and “my smart young lady.”
La chaleur envahit le bureau où se dérou: The heat fills the office where the interview is taking place. Annie waves her red fan, decorated with little yellow drawings, to cool off. Eager to get back to her cooking, she stands up quickly as soon as the camera turns off. Time to get back to the stove!
